role: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, project sponsor and EIS preparer
stance_basis: HUD authored the EIS, prepared responses defending the project's analysis, and explicitly rebutted DOT objections to justify including the Downtown Expressway as a relevant environmental consideration
summary: HUD is the project sponsor and EIS preparer for the Randolph Urban Renewal Project, and in this chapter it responds to comments from other agencies. HUD defends its methodology, particularly its decision to analyze the Downtown Expressway's impacts on the project area, citing NEPA requirements and EPA confirmation. HUD also addresses requests for additional air quality data, traffic documentation, and noise analysis clarifications, explaining constraints while maintaining the validity of its assessments.
complaint_summary: HUD explains that it was unable to obtain peak-hour volume and air dispersion modeling data for the Downtown Expressway due to lack of cooperation from the Richmond Metropolitan Authority (citing litigation) and insufficient staff and hardware capacity, while noting that proposed automobile emission controls may reduce pollution impacts.

statement.text:
The Area Office has made efforts to obtain the above requested information but to no avail. The Downtown Expressway as it passes through the Randolph project area is being constructed by the Richmond Metropolitan Authority without any state or federal funds. As such the Department of Highways has not been able to provide the Area Office with PHV and average speed figures for two years following highway completion. The Richmond Metropolitan Authority was contacted relative to this information but because of current litigation against the Downtown Expressway it could not provide the information.
While the design year figures are available the Area Office is not able to calculate CO concentrations because it does not have the staff and hardware capability to complete the analysis. The Virginia Department of Highways has been contacted relative to the use of its facilities but preliminary investigations have indicated that there would be a charge for the use of the program and facilities. Subsequent contacts have indicated that the Department of Highway's facilities would not be available to HUD for an indefinite period because of a substantial backlog of the Department's own work.
While the Area Office agrees that it would be desirable to obtain these ratings there is little it can do in project design that would effectively reduce the impacts of air pollution other than the measures, such as air conditioning, that have been proposed. Hopefully, the proposed controls on automobile emissions will be effectuated within the next five years. If so, this action should have a much more positive impact on the reduction of pollutants than anything HUD can propose.
